title: Using Multimedia for E-Learning https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jcal.12197
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 19, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page summarises Richard Mayer's synthesis of twelve evidence-based principles for multimedia e-learning design, organised around cognitive theory's three demands on working memory: extraneous processing (unnecessary cognitive load to eliminate), essential processing (the complexity of the material itself, which needs managing), and generative processing (the effort of actively making sense of material, which needs encouraging). Mayer reviews empirical evidence, including effect sizes, for each principle. On extraneous load, the guidance includes cutting irrelevant material, avoiding on-screen text that duplicates narration, and placing labels next to the graphics they describe. On essential processing, the guidance includes letting learners control pacing through segmented, user-paced lessons and pre-training key vocabulary before a lesson. On generative processing, the guidance includes using a conversational rather than formal register and human rather than synthesized voices. Barton notes that these boundary conditions matter -- for example, personalization tends to help lower-prior-knowledge learners more than higher-prior-knowledge ones -- and that Mayer calls for further classroom-based research to test the robustness of these principles over time.
points: The multimedia principle: people learn better from words and pictures together than from words alone, which is the foundational rationale for the whole framework.
To cut extraneous load, exclude irrelevant material, avoid duplicating narration as on-screen text, and place printed labels next to the graphics they describe.
To manage essential processing, segment lessons into user-paced chunks and pre-train key vocabulary before the lesson begins.
To boost generative processing, use a conversational register and a human (not synthesized) narrating voice.
The principles' effectiveness has boundary conditions -- for instance, personalization benefits lower-prior-knowledge learners more than higher-prior-knowledge ones.
quotes: The rationale for computer-based multimedia instruction is that people learn better from words and pictures than from words alone, which can be called the multimedia principle
Exclude extraneous material from multimedia lessons. For example, students scored better on tests when interesting but irrelevant facts were excluded from lessons on a range of scientific topics
Present graphics and narration rather than graphics, narration, and on-screen text that repeats the narration

Place printed words near corresponding parts of the graphic. For example, students learned better when words were integrated with graphics, rather than separated, in lessons about scientific processes
Break multimedia lessons into user-paced segments. Studies show that students performed better on tests when they could learn in segments, clicking to move to the next segment when they were ready

Present words in spoken form rather than printed on the screen. Research suggests that students tend to learn better when words are presented as narration rather than on-screen text in multimedia lessons
Use recordings of human voices rather than machine-synthesized voices. For instance, one study showed that people learned better when lessons about scientific topics were narrated by a human voice
